cards.text: Israel is in the middle of a battle with the Philistines. Saul, Israel's king, has put his troops under an oath. And that day, the men of Israel are in distress.

cards.question: Saul's oath puts a curse on any soldier who does what before evening?

cards.text: So not one soldier tastes any food, and the troops head into a forest. Friend, I can't even sprinkle a cookie on an empty stomach, and these men are swinging SWORDS.

cards.question: In the forest, the troops find ___ on the ground.

cards.text: Flowing honey, right there, and not ONE soldier puts his hand to his mouth. Friend, drop warm cookies in front of me after a day like that, and my mustache grabs one before my brain even gets a vote.

cards.question: Why won't the hungry troops touch the honey?

cards.text: But Jonathan, Saul's son, never heard that his father bound the people with the oath. Nobody told him a thing.

cards.question: Jonathan walks right past the honey and leaves it alone, just like the rest of the troops.

cards.text: One taste off the end of his staff, and Jonathan's eyes brighten, the same face I make when the first batch comes out of the oven. Then a soldier tells him about the oath.

cards.question: The soldier tells Jonathan that the oath is why the people are ___.

cards.text: Jonathan says, "My father has brought trouble to the land," and points to his own bright eyes. All that, he says, from a little honey.

cards.question: Jonathan says the slaughter of the Philistines would have been much greater if the troops had done what?

cards.text: Israel strikes down the Philistines from Michmash all the way to Aijalon. And by then, the people are very faint.

cards.question: When the starving troops rush to the plunder of sheep and cattle, what do they do?

answers.text: Eat meat with the blood still in it
Wait for Saul to divide it all up
Burn it as an offering to the LORD

cards.question: Someone reports to Saul that the troops are sinning against the LORD by eating meat with the blood still in it.

cards.text: Saul says, "You have broken faith," and orders a large stone rolled over at once.

cards.question: Saul tells each man to bring his ox or sheep to that spot, slaughter it there, and then eat.

cards.text: So that night, everyone brings his ox and slaughters it there. Then Saul builds something for the LORD.

cards.question: What does Saul build for the LORD?
It was the ___ time Saul had built an altar to the LORD.

cards.text: Saul's ready to go again: down after the Philistines by night, plundering them until dawn and leaving no man alive. "Do what seems good to you," the troops tell him.

cards.question: Before they march, the priest speaks up. What does he say they must do first?

cards.text: So Saul asks God: should he go down after the Philistines? Will God give them into the hand of Israel?

cards.question: God answers Saul's question that same day.

cards.text: God is silent, so Saul calls in the leaders of the troops to investigate how this sin has occurred today. Friend, I've been on the wrong end of a kitchen investigation, and flour on your mustache is NOT a good alibi.

cards.question: Saul swears by the LORD who saves Israel that whoever sinned must die, "even if it is my son ___, he must die!"
After Saul's oath, the troops speak up and tell him what Jonathan did.

cards.text: Not one of them says a word. So Saul puts all Israel on one side, and himself and Jonathan on the other.

cards.question: Saul asks the LORD to answer with Urim if the fault is with Saul or Jonathan, and Thummim if it's with the men of Israel. Which side is selected?
Saul casts the lot between himself and Jonathan, and the lot falls on Saul.

cards.text: Saul commands Jonathan to tell what he did. Jonathan says he only tasted a little honey with the end of his staff. "And now I must die?"

cards.question: How does Saul answer his son Jonathan?

answers.text: He swears Jonathan will surely die
He says the oath doesn't count for him
He tells the priest to decide it

cards.question: Then the people speak up to Saul. Why do they say Jonathan must never die?

answers.text: He brought a great deliverance for Israel
He promised never to do it again
He is the son of the king

cards.question: So the people ___ Jonathan, and he did not die.
After all that, what does Saul do about the Philistines?

cards.text: From the time Saul takes the kingship, he fights enemies on every side: the Moabites, the Ammonites, the Edomites, the kings of Zobah and the Philistines. Wherever he turns, he routes them, and he fights valiantly against the Amalekites and delivers Israel from its plunderers.
Then comes Saul's family: his sons Jonathan, Ishvi and Malchishua, his daughters Merab and Michal, and his wife Ahinoam. His army commander is Abner, son of Saul's uncle Ner.
The war with the Philistines stays fierce for all of Saul's days, so whenever he notices a strong or brave man, he enlists him. And friend, Saul's story? It's not finished yet.

findings.problem: Stop 2, card 6 quotes "even if it is my son ___, he must die!", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: The joke says "these men are swinging SWORDS." That presents the Israelite troops having swords as a fact. 1 Samuel 13:22 says that on the day of battle not a sword or spear could be found in the hands of the troops, except for Saul and Jonathan. The text never says the troops gained swords, so the line risks contradicting Scripture. Use a comparison that doesn't make a claim about their weapons.

rule.text: Papa Dorin can retell in his own words and fill in what the text clearly implies. Scene-setting details are fine. He never says anything the text shows is wrong.

findings.problem: The question calls them "the starving troops." Verse 31 says the people were "very faint." "Starving" pushes past what the text says, and it isn't one of Papa Dorin's own jokes. Use "faint" or "very faint" instead.

rule.text: Don't stretch the text. Exaggerate only in his own jokes.

findings.problem: The card opens with "God is silent," which comes from verse 37. It cites only 1 Samuel 14:38. The citation should be 1 Samuel 14:37-38.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: The card opens with "Not one of them says a word," which comes from verse 39. It cites only 1 Samuel 14:40. The citation should be 1 Samuel 14:39-40.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: "So Saul puts all Israel on one side" makes the troops' silence the reason for Saul's next step. Verse 40 only says "Then Saul said" and doesn't link the two. Use "Then" instead of "So."

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The statement says "Saul casts the lot." In verse 42, Saul says "Cast the lot between me and my son Jonathan." He gives the order, and the text doesn't say who casts it. Reword it, for example: "Saul has the lot cast between himself and Jonathan, and the lot falls on Saul."

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: "Wherever he turns, he routes them" misspells the BSB's "routed." "Routes" means sending something along a path, which is not what verse 47 says. It should be "routs them."

rule.text: Papa Dorin can retell in his own words and fill in what the text clearly implies. Scene-setting details are fine. He never says anything the text shows is wrong.

findings.problem: The card cites 1 Samuel 14:49-51 but tells nothing from verse 51 (Kish and Ner were sons of Abiel). Either add a short detail from verse 51, such as Saul's father Kish, or cite 1 Samuel 14:49-50.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: Stop 2 has only one joke (card 5) in 18 cards. Cards 1, 3, 11, 16, 17 and 18 read as plain narration. Several moments could hold a real laugh without muddying a fact: the troops saying "Do what seems good to you" a second time, the people's flat "Never!" to the king, or Saul calling off the chase after all that.

rule.text: When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
